subject: science
title: GCSE Science diagnostic
curriculum: DfE GCSE combined science subject content (2015), shared by AQA, Edexcel, OCR and WJEC. Also suitable for IGCSE.

skills.name: Biology
skills.why: Biology is a third of GCSE science and rewards clear understanding over memorising.
skills.strong: {name} knows cells, transport and genetics well and can explain biological processes.
skills.developing: {name} knows the key facts but is less confident explaining processes such as enzymes and inheritance.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with core biology such as cells and the circulatory system. These ideas come up again and again, so they are worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will link the key facts together so the explanations make sense, not just the words.

skills.name: Chemistry
skills.why: Chemistry is a third of GCSE science, and its calculations are where many marks are won or lost.
skills.strong: {name} understands atoms and bonding and handles chemical calculations confidently.
skills.developing: {name} knows atomic structure but finds bonding and chemical calculations harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with atoms, elements and bonding. The rest of chemistry builds on these, so they come first.
skills.next_step: We will build from atomic structure up to relative mass and moles, one step at a time.

skills.name: Physics
skills.why: Physics questions often need an equation used correctly, so method matters as much as knowledge.
skills.strong: {name} uses physics equations confidently, including unit conversions.
skills.developing: {name} can use simple equations but slips with harder ones and with converting units.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident using physics equations such as speed and current. These are reliable marks once the method is secure.
skills.next_step: We will practise a clear routine for every equation: write it, substitute, check the units.

skills.name: Working scientifically
skills.why: At least 15% of GCSE science marks test practical skills, and data handling comes up in every topic.
skills.strong: {name} understands variables, repeat readings and uncertainty well.
skills.developing: {name} knows the basics of fair testing but is less sure handling data and uncertainty.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with variables and handling results. These skills are tested in every topic, so they are worth securing.
skills.next_step: We will practise reading results, spotting anomalies and working with data.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant cell is where photosynthesis takes place?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explain: Na, from the Latin natrium. S is sulfur.

questions.stem: What is the unit of force?
questions.explain: Force is measured in newtons (N). Joules are energy, watts are power, pascals are pressure.

questions.stem: In an experiment, what is the name for the variable that you choose to change?
questions.explain: The independent variable is changed; the dependent variable is measured; control variables are kept the same.

questions.stem: What is the name of the process in which water moves across a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one?
questions.explain: Osmosis. Diffusion is the general term for particles; osmosis is specifically water across a membrane.

questions.stem: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23. 11 is the atomic number.

questions.stem: A car travels 150 m in 10 s. What is its average speed?
questions.explain: 150 ÷ 10 = 15 m/s. 1500 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Why should a scientist repeat an experiment several times?
options: To check the results are repeatable and to spot anomalies
questions.explain: Repeats show whether results are repeatable and let you identify and exclude anomalous readings.

questions.stem: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back. Valves are not vessels.

questions.stem: What type of bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal, for example in sodium chloride?
questions.explain: Metal atoms lose electrons and non-metal atoms gain them, forming ions held by ionic bonds. Covalent is non-metal to non-metal.

questions.stem:
A student times a trolley rolling down a ramp four times:
12.1 s, 12.3 s, 15.8 s, 12.2 s

Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean time?
questions.explain: 15.8 s is the anomaly. (12.1 + 12.3 + 12.2) ÷ 3 = 36.6 ÷ 3 = 12.2 s. Including it gives 13.1 s.

questions.stem: A current of 2 A flows through a 6 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the resistor?
questions.explain: V = I × R = 2 × 6 = 12 V. 3 comes from dividing.

questions.stem: A graph of the extension of a spring against the force applied is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
options: Extension is directly proportional to force
Force and extension are not related
questions.explain: A straight line through the origin shows direct proportion (Hooke's law).

questions.stem: Two parents are both heterozygous for a characteristic (Bb). What percentage of their offspring would be expected to be homozygous recessive (bb)?
questions.explain: Punnett square: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. One in four is bb = 25%. 75% is the dominant phenotype.

questions.stem:
What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of carbon dioxide, CO₂?
Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16
questions.explain: 12 + (2 × 16) = 44. 28 counts only one oxygen.

questions.stem:
A ball of mass 2 kg moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
Use: kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed²
questions.explain: ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. 3 forgets to square the speed; 18 forgets the half.

questions.stem:
A student measures the length of a spring three times:
4.2 cm, 4.6 cm, 4.4 cm

The uncertainty is half the range. What is the uncertainty?
questions.explain: Range = 4.6 − 4.2 = 0.4 cm. Half of that is 0.2 cm.

questions.stem: A 1200 W kettle is switched on for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
questions.explain: Time must be in seconds: 2 min = 120 s. E = P × t = 1200 × 120 = 144 000 J. 2400 forgets to convert minutes.

questions.stem: Enzymes stop working when the temperature gets too high. Explain why.

rubric.criterion: The shape of the active site changes, or the enzyme is denatured
So the substrate no longer fits the active site (and the reaction cannot be catalysed)

questions.explain: 'The enzyme dies' earns nothing: enzymes are not alive. Look for active site shape and substrate fit.

questions.stem:
How many moles are there in 88 g of carbon dioxide?
The Mr of carbon dioxide is 44.
questions.explain: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 88 ÷ 44 = 2 mol. 3872 multiplies instead.
